entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The University of Melbourne, founded in 1853 as Australia's second oldest university (after Sydney, 1850), is Australia's highest-ranked research university and a member of the Group of Eight research universities that produce the majority of Australia's research output. The university's sandstone Gothic buildings in Parkville, Melbourne, and its 220 Nobel laureates, prime ministers, and vice-chancellors among alumni make it the institutional center of Australian intellectual and professional life for 170 years.

The University of Melbourne was established in the aftermath of the Victoria gold rush (1851) as the young colony's cultural statement — building elaborate Gothic Revival buildings by German architect Friedrich Kawerau to rival Oxford and Cambridge. The university's medical school (established 1862) was Australia's first and produced the Nobel laureates who developed penicillin applications, cancer research, and immunology advances. Melbourne's Law School produced four of Australia's seven prime ministers since 1975.

The Melbourne Model (2008) — replacing undergraduate specialization with broad generalist bachelor degrees followed by professional graduate schools — was Australia's most radical university reform since federation, modeled on American liberal arts traditions. The model influenced Australian universities nationally and its graduate professional schools in law, medicine, education, and engineering are now ranked among Asia-Pacific's finest. The university's BioMedical Precinct — co-located with the Royal Melbourne Hospital and Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research — creates an integrated medical research ecosystem.
